content: Clotrimazole is a medication used to treat fungal infections caused by yeast, including infections of the vagina, mouth, and skin. It is effective for conditions such as athlete's foot, jock itch, and ringworm. In some cases, it may also be prescribed to prevent oral thrush in certain patients. If you have questions about other potential uses, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Clotrimazole is available in various forms, including creams, lotions, and solutions for application to the skin; lozenges (troches) that dissolve in the mouth; and vaginal tablets or creams for insertion into the vagina. The specific dosing regimen depends on the condition being treated. For oral thrush, it is typically used five times daily for 14 days. For skin infections, it is applied twice daily (morning and evening) for 2 to 8 weeks. For vaginal infections, it is used once daily at bedtime for either 3 or 7 days. Always follow the instructions on the package or prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the medication exactly as directed, and do not alter the dose or frequency without medical advice. When using the topical cream, lotion, or solution, clean the affected area thoroughly, allow it to dry, and then gently rub in the medication until most of it disappears. Use only enough to cover the infected area, and wash your hands after application. For lozenges, place one in your mouth and allow it to dissolve slowly over 15 to 30 minutes. Do not chew or swallow the lozenge whole. For vaginal cream or tablets, follow the instructions provided with the product. Typically, you will: 1. Fill the applicator with the cream to the indicated level or prepare the tablet by wetting it with lukewarm water and placing it on the applicator. 2. Lie on your back with your knees bent and spread apart. 3. Insert the applicator high into the vagina (unless you are pregnant, in which case you should insert it gently). If you encounter resistance, stop and consult your doctor. 4. Push the plunger to release the medication, then withdraw the applicator. 5. Dispose of a disposable applicator or clean a reusable one with soap and warm water after each use. 6. Wash your hands immediately to prevent spreading the infection. The vaginal cream or tablets are best applied at bedtime, as the medication works most effectively when you remain lying down. Avoid getting up after application, except to wash your hands. You may use a sanitary napkin to protect your clothing, but do not use tampons, as they can absorb the medication. Do not douche unless instructed by your doctor. Continue using the medication even if your symptoms improve, and do not stop treatment without consulting your doctor. If you are using clotrimazole during your menstrual period, continue the treatment as directed. If you are using clotrimazole cream, lotion, or solution without a prescription, apply it for 4 weeks for athlete's foot and 2 weeks for jock itch or ringworm. If your symptoms do not improve within this time, stop using the medication and consult a doctor or pharmacist. If you are using clotrimazole vaginal cream or tablets without a prescription and this is your first experience with vaginal itching or discomfort, consult a doctor before use. If you have previously been diagnosed with a yeast infection and experience the same symptoms, use the product as directed for 3 or 7 consecutive days, preferably at night. If symptoms persist beyond this period or return within 2 months, contact your doctor. Before using clotrimazole, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to clotrimazole or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs you are taking, including antibiotics and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of liver disease, immune system problems, HIV/AIDS, diabetes, or alcohol abuse. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using clotrimazole, contact your doctor immediately. Additionally, let your doctor know if you consume alcohol. If you miss a dose, take or apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to make up for a missed one. Clotrimazole may cause side effects. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience itching, burning, irritation, redness, swelling, stomach pain, fever, foul-smelling discharge (if using the vaginal product), or upset stomach or vomiting (with lozenges). Serious side effects should be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store clotrimazole in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture, and do not freeze it. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. Clotrimazole cream, lotion, and solution are for external use only. Avoid contact with the eyes, and do not swallow these forms of the medication. Vaginal tablets and creams should not be swallowed. If you have a vaginal infection, avoid sexual intercourse during treatment. Note that the cream may weaken latex products such as condoms or diaphragms, so do not use these within 72 hours of applying the medication. Wear clean cotton underwear, and avoid synthetic fabrics like nylon or rayon. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refills. If your symptoms persist after completing treatment, contact your doctor. Clotrimazole is sold under various brand names, including Fungoid® Solution, Gyne-Lotrimin®, Lotrimin®, and Mycelex® Troche. Combination products, such as Lotrisone®, contain clotrimazole and betamethasone dipropionate.
